newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain markets unruffled by Sweden missing EMU star.
newsitem.headline: Spain markets unruffled by Sweden missing EMU star.

text.p: Spanish markets will brush aside fellow peripheral nation Sweden's decision to skip the launch of Europe's single currency, analysts said on Tuesday.

"This is an issue sui generis (unique to Sweden)," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid. "The market already smelled something otherwise the yield spread wouldn't be above Spain."

On Tuesday, Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson, in the first statement of his ruling party views on EMU membership, said the country would not join Europe's economic and monetary union at the proposed start in January 1999.
Although markets once grouped Sweden and Spain together as members of the EMU fringe, Spain's one-year-old conservative government has taken a different route.

Spain turned the pursuit of a spot on the team of euro founders into the cornerstone of its European policy, tightening the budget, deregulating industries and was rewarded with lower inflation and interest rates and a steady currency.

"It's a little early but in principle I don't think that affects (Spain). For the process, the key countries are France and Germany. The UK has already said 'no' and now Sweden and Denmark are also keeping to themselves," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
Spanish bond futures ended the day up 72 basis points to 115.91, rising on a short-squeeze and following sister markets, while disregarding the Swedish news.
The peseta also shrugged aside the Swedish decision, trading little changed at 84.48/50 per mark late in the day.
